newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bugging row highlights president's power.
newsitem.headline: French bugging row highlights president's power.

text.p: Reports that the late president Francois Mitterrand personally ordered widespread illegal telephone-tapping sparked a call on Friday for France's head of state to be liable to criminal investigation.

Secret files from Mitterrand's anti-terrorist unit, published by newspapers on Thursday, have prompted virtually no comment from his Socialist party or from the ruling centre-right coalition amid speculation that phone-tapping is still common.

Patrick Devedjian, a deputy for President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR, told the daily Le Monde that the head of state "cannot be investigated, save for cases of 'high treason' which no text defines.
"The president is therefore above the law. This situation therefore poses a problem even beyond Francois Mitterrand's behaviour," Devedjian said.
Le Monde and the magazine L'Express published what they said were extracts from files seized by DST counter-espionage officers and investigating magistrates in February.

The archives, stored in a garage outside Paris rented by the unit's former head, Christian Prouteau, included recordings of telephone-taps, demands for presidential favours and memos on terrorism suspects.
Both reports said many notes destined for Mitterrand carried his laconic handwritten comment: "Vu" (Seen).

"The Fifth Republic is a monarchical, albeit republican system in which the president does not follow common rules," said Le Monde journalist Edwy Plenel, whose phone was tapped when he investigated the sinking of the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior by the French secret service in 1985.
"I would like to be certain that practices do not continue today," Plenel said.
Investigating magistrate Jean-Paul Valat questioned Prouteau, who invoked official secrets rules, for eight hours on Thursday.

Prouteau, two former senior government officials, and three members of the since-disbanded unit are under investigation over the alleged telephone tapping of dozens of politicians, writers, lawyers and journalists without judicial permission.

France's supreme court last month rejected a bid to stop the investigation, ruling that the statute of limitations in invasion of privacy cases only applied from the moment the offence was discovered, not the date when it was committed.
Among those whose phones were tapped was actress Carole Bouquet, said to be amorously pursued by a senior presidential aide, jealous of her other admirers.
The former head of Mitterrand's private office, Gilles Menage, has acknowledged the unit carried out wiretapping but said it was strictly for national security purposes.
Le Monde reported Prime Minister Alain Juppe had rejected his demand that official secrecy rules be waived so that he could defend himself. There was no immediate confirmation.
However, L'Express said the files made clear a key purpose was to protect Mitterrand's own private life, and in particular the secrecy surrounding his illegitimate daughter, Mazarine.
Legal wiretaps can only by approved by magistrates in criminal cases or to protect national security, prevent terrorist threats or safeguard essential scientific or economic information.
